submitted_caption: Figure 1. mFLOW-Seq workflow overview. Schematic illustration of the mFLOW-Seq pipeline: sample collection (vaginal swab, cervical brush, endometrial biopsy), microbial enrichment by differential centrifugation, DAPI membrane-integrity gating, IgA-PE/IgM-APC/IgG-FITC labelling, flow cytometry sorting into five fractions (IgA⁺, IgM⁺, IgG⁺, IgA⁺/IgM⁺ double-positive, unbound), and V1–V9 16S rRNA gene sequencing. n = 16 participants; 292 total fresh and frozen fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-sorted fractions. Bacterial-sized events were first identified using forward- and side-scatter properties relative to buffer and background controls, followed by fluorescence-based gating to exclude non-bacterial debris and host-derived particles prior to identification of DAPI⁻ membrane-intact bacteria (SYTO9⁺/PI⁻ used for cross-validation) and immunoglobulin-bound bacterial fractions. Images were generated using BioRender.
changes: Replaces viability/cross-validation and variance-ranking labels with operational DAPI selection, separate pilots, correct PRE/unbound distinction and cautious interpretation. Original vector illustration/image streams preserved.

submitted_caption: Figure 2. Alpha diversity across Ig fractions and anatomical sites stratified by vaginal microbiota status. Box plots of Shannon entropy (H’), Simpson (1−D), taxon richness, and Pielou’s evenness (J’) across pre-sorted, IgA⁺, IgM⁺, and IgG⁺ fractions for vagina (blue), cervix (green), and endometrium (red), stratified by vaginal microbiota status (Lactobacillus-dominant vs. vaginally dysbiotic). Kruskal–Wallis significance annotations are shown per group per panel (*p < 0.05, ns = not significant). Individual data points are overlaid. n = 9 Lactobacillus-dominant, n = 7 vaginally dysbiotic participants.
changes: Original multi-metric/clinical-group boxplots and pooled significance labels replaced by preparation-connected Shannon points; revised mixed model uses woman and preparation random intercepts, phase adjustment/subset and sensitivity checks.

submitted_caption: Figure 3. Beta diversity ordination: PCoA and NMDS of Bray–Curtis dissimilarities. PCoA (top row) and NMDS (bottom row) ordinations of Bray–Curtis dissimilarities coloured by anatomical site (column 1), immunoglobulin fraction (column 2), vaginal microbiota status (column 3), and storage method (column 4). Ellipses represent 95% confidence intervals per group. PERMANOVA results (R², p-value) are annotated in each panel. n = 292 total flow-cytometry-sorted fractions; PERMANOVA analyses were based on n = 149 post-QC samples. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ns = not significant.
changes: Original PCoA/NMDS grid and unrestricted PERMANOVA labels replaced by participant-connected PCoA. Focused tests, matching and dispersion qualifications are reported in tables; the plotted ordination is descriptive.

submitted_caption: Figure 4. Immunoglobulin-binding profiles: flow cytometry-sorted cell counts and sequencing read distributions. (Top row) Violin plots of sorted bacterial event counts (log₁₀) per Ig fraction (IgA⁺, IgM⁺, IgG⁺) across vagina, cervix, and endometrium. (Bottom row) Violin plots of 16S rRNA gene sequencing read counts (log₁₀) per Ig fraction and site. Individual participant data points are overlaid; horizontal bars indicate medians. Statistical comparisons between IgA⁺ and IgM⁺ flow cytometry event counts are annotated above each top-row panel (*** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, ns = not significant; Wilcoxon signed-rank test); sequencing read comparisons (bottom row) were not significant at any site. Sample sizes indicated within each violin; note logarithmic y-axis. IgM⁺ fractions at cervical and endometrial sites frequently reached the preset sorting limit of 1×10⁶ events, so the true size of these populations may be underestimated in the plotted counts. Event counts reflect cytometric detection of bacterial-sized DAPI⁻ events and should be interpreted as approximate abundance of membrane-intact bacterial events rather than absolute cell numbers.
changes: Original sorted-event yields and sequencing-count violins replaced by Ig-gate percentages reconstructed from original PDF gate counts divided by their recorded DAPI-negative parent. One woman/site; pointwise bootstrap intervals. Sorting yield, acquired events and sequence counts remain distinct.

submitted_caption: Figure 5. Differential Ig-coating of the microbiota: IgA vs. IgM taxon enrichment across the FRT. (A) Heatmap of mean relative abundance (%) for all retained taxa across Ig fractions (IgA, IgM, pre-sorted) and anatomical sites (vagina, cervix, endometrium). Colour scale: yellow→dark red = 0–60%+. (B) Diverging bar plots showing log₂(IgA/IgM) ratio for individual taxa per anatomical site. Orange bars: IgA-enriched; purple bars: IgM-enriched; dot size proportional to pre-sorted abundance. (C) Bubble chart of mean relative abundance in IgA fraction (x-axis) vs. IgM fraction (y-axis) across all sites. Bubble size: pre-sorted abundance; colour: anatomical site (orange = Endometrium, blue = Vagina, green = Cervix); border colour: IgA-enriched vs. IgM-enriched. Taxa above the diagonal are IgM-biased; below are IgA-biased. Dashed line: equal IgA/IgM abundance.
changes: Original heatmap/pooled log-ratio/bubble composite replaced by site-specific matched IgA/IgM relative representation with equal-woman weighting, detection counts and bootstrap intervals. It is not a per-cell binding probability.

submitted_caption: Figure 6. Microbial community differences by vaginal microbiota status. (A) Strip plots of key taxon relative abundances (log-scale) in participants with Lactobacillus-dominant vaginal microbiota (blue) and vaginal dysbiosis (red) across vagina, cervix, and endometrium. Taxon labels denote the following species: iners = Lactobacillus iners; crispatus = Lactobacillus crispatus; vaginalis [S] = Sneathia vaginalis; vaginalis [G] = Gardnerella vaginalis; vaginae = Fannyhessea vaginae; buccalis = Prevotella buccalis. (B) Shannon diversity boxplots per site and vaginal microbiota status. (C) PCoA of Bray–Curtis dissimilarities in pre-sorted communities per site, coloured by vaginal microbiota status. PERMANOVA R² and p-values are annotated. Lactobacillus-dominant (n = 9), vaginally dysbiotic (n = 7).

submitted_caption: Figure 7. Fresh vs. cryopreserved sample comparison: taxon composition and Ig-binding are preserved. (Top row) Bar plots showing mean ± SD of Lactobacillus spp. relative abundance in IgA⁺, IgM⁺, and pre-sorted fractions for fresh (solid) vs. frozen (hatched) samples across vagina, cervix, and endometrium. Individual participant values are overlaid as dots. Sample sizes per group are annotated (n = fresh/frozen). Cervix frozen bars represent a single participant (n = 1); no SD is shown and no statistical comparison was performed for this site. (Bottom row) Heatmaps of mean relative abundance (%) for the eight dominant taxa per anatomical site (columns selected from the species-level taxon abundance table) across IgA⁺, IgM⁺, and pre-sorted fractions in fresh and frozen specimens. White horizontal lines separate fraction groups. Colour scale: cream → orange → dark red = 0–80%. Vagina: fresh n = 6, frozen n = 4; cervix: fresh n = 9, frozen n = 1; endometrium: fresh n = 9, frozen n = 6.
changes: Original fresh/frozen mean plots and heatmaps replaced by descriptive per-woman profiles with corrected group denominators and shared heatmap scale. General preservation-equivalence conclusions removed; HUT99 same-biopsy pairing is described.

submitted_caption: Figure 8. IgA versus IgM taxon enrichment by anatomical site: lollipop plot. Lollipop plots showing the difference in mean relative abundance between IgA⁺ and IgM⁺ fractions [IgA − IgM (%)] for all retained taxa across vagina (left), cervix (centre), and endometrium (right). Positive values (orange bars and dots) indicate IgA-enriched taxa; negative values (purple) indicate IgM-enriched taxa. Dot size is proportional to pre-sorted mean relative abundance, providing context for the immunological significance of each enrichment. Taxa are ordered by IgA–IgM enrichment difference (most IgA-enriched at top, most IgM-enriched at bottom). Representative enriched taxa are annotated with abbreviated italic labels. In the cervix panel, Mageeibacillus indolicus† (grey, dashed dot border) is shown for transparency but was excluded from all primary analyses as a confirmed reagent contaminant (Supplementary Information, S-MM5). Data are from the decontaminated, abundance-filtered species-level taxon table (39 taxa; n = 15 IgA⁺ samples, n = 15 IgM⁺ samples for vagina; n = 9/9 for cervix; n = 14/15 for endometrium).

submitted_caption: Figure 9. Advanced multivariate analysis: CLR-PCA biplot, PERMANOVA effect sizes, and spatial Ig gradient. (A) CLR-PCA biplot of all samples (circles, coloured by anatomical site: blue = Vagina, green = Cervix, red = Endometrium) and species loadings (arrows, labelled for dominant taxa). PC1 (36.9%) separates endometrial from vaginal communities; PC2 (14.1%) captures additional community variation. (B) PERMANOVA effect-size barplot showing R² (variance explained) for each driver: Ig fraction (orange, R² = 0.078**), Anatomical site (blue, R² = 0.057**), Vaginal microbiota status (red, R² = 0.015*), Storage method (grey, R² = 0.012, ns); n = 999 permutations. (C) Spatial Ig gradient bar plots for seven key taxa across IgA, IgM, and IgG fractions at vagina, cervix, and endometrium. Bar colour: anatomical site (blue = Vagina, green = Cervix, red = Endometrium); bar groups: Ig fraction (IgA, IgM, IgG). The panel illustrates that L. iners is the dominant taxon across multiple fractions, reaching its highest abundance in the endometrial IgM fraction (82.5%), while Sneathia vaginalis is most abundant in IgA fractions at vaginal (17.2%) and cervical (22.7%) sites, consistent with its IgA coating score of 0.999.

submitted_caption: Figure 10. Fluorescence microscopy confirms morphologically intact bacterial cells before and after flow cytometry sorting. Fluorescence microscopy images (SYTO™ 9 staining, green channel) of pre-sorted (panels A–C, G–I, M–O) and FACS-sorted (panels D–F, J–L, P–R) fractions from vaginal swab (row 1, orange tab), cervix (row 2, purple tab), and endometrium (row 3, teal tab). Pre-sorted panels show mixed populations including large host epithelial cells (large, intensely bright round structures) alongside smaller bacterial-sized events. Post-sort panels confirm successful isolation of morphologically intact bacterial cells (rods and cocci, 0.5–3 μm) with no observable host cell contamination in the imaged fields. White arrows indicate individual bacterial cells. Scale bars = 10 μm. Images acquired on a Zeiss Axio Observer, 100× oil-immersion objective (NA 1.4). Representative images shown; n ≥ 3 participants per anatomical site.
